Inundate

/IN-uhn-dayt/ - the stress falls on IN · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Inundate means to flood or overwhelm with a huge amount.

The spring melt inundated the low pastures, and the ewes spent a week grazing the hill.

Worked Example

When the registrar posted the wrong grade cutoff, appeals inundated her office within a day — a stack by nine, a second clerk by noon, a locked door by Friday.

Inundate began as water — unda is Latin for 'wave' — and still does that literal work, but its daily job is volume that overwhelms capacity: appeals, complaints, entries. Swamp and deluge are its close kin; sprinkle-scale words like dampen never qualify.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

swamp: To swamp is to bury something under more than it can handle -- the informal twin of inundate, at home in speech and email. Inundate does the same work in formal writing, and keeps the literal flood sense alive. Your inbox gets swamped; a report says the office was inundated.

deluge: A deluge pours down in torrents -- the word is more dramatic than inundate, painting the volume as a biblical downpour, water or mail alike. Inundate is the standard, neutral term for volume beyond capacity. Use deluge when you want the flood to sound spectacular.

engulf: To engulf is to swallow whole -- the thing disappears inside what covers it, a boat inside a wave, a house inside flames. Inundate overwhelms a thing's capacity while it struggles on above the flood. If the victim has vanished entirely, engulf is the word.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

drain: to draw the flood away

parch: to dry out entirely — the opposite extreme

Where it sits · how completely it gets covered — dampen → soak → inundate

dampen vs. inundate: To dampen is the lightest touch of water — it stops a long way short of inundate, which buries a thing under it.

soak vs. inundate: To soak drenches something through, yet still stops short of inundate, which covers and overwhelms it entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: onto, over (not the negative in-)

Root — -und-

Root — -und-: wave (Latin unda)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: verb

Put it together

Put it together: Directional again: in- ('onto, over') + unda ('wave') + -ate — waves rolled over it. Read it as 'not undated' and you get nonsense; the un- you think you see is just the first syllable of unda. The same wave rolls through undulate, this unit's other unda word.

Use the root in a new word: undulate

Use the root in a new word: undulate: Undulate — taught later in this very unit — is unda's other child: what inundates rolls over you in waves; what undulates simply moves like one.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Inundate is the standard word for volume beyond capacity, literal floodwater or five hundred emails. Swamp says the same thing informally; deluge is more dramatic. If the amount is merely large but manageable, you were busy, not inundated.
